utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Alex Demirdjian, and this morning we're joined by Stephen Bailey, and, as usual, Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the witness comes in, we've been alerted by the Court Officer that Mr. Zecevic has something to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday, on page 95, I understand Your Honours' comments and is an invitation to provide the authority for the submission on the -- on the objection I made, if you remember, concerning the introduction of new evidence by the Office of the Prosecutor at this stage of the proceedings. And I did research, and there is the Appeals Chamber decision dated 26th February 2009, Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. case. It's a decision on the interlocutory appeal against the Trial Chamber's decision on presentation of documents by the Prosecution in cross-examination of Defence witnesses. Since we are pressed with time, I don't think that there is any need at this point to make additional submissions, but I just wanted to give this reference to the Trial Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What was the date again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 26th February 2009. The Appeals Chamber decision in Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, because, as Mr. Zecevic says, the pressures of time, Your Honours, I'd ask Your Honours to adjourn this particular argument to sometime next week or possibly on Monday, depending on how much re-examination Mr. Zecevic has, because although we've dealt with and we've argued and we're awaiting a ruling on the Defence request for early disclosure of any documents that we propose to use in cross-examination, this is a slightly different point which hasn't really been argued; namely, whether the Prosecution, in its cross-examination, is limited to cross-examination as to credit or can advance its case through cross-examination, in other words, by producing evidence that hasn't been used before. So if I may, if I could ask Your Honours simply to adjourn that to a convenient moment next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course. We weren't expecting you to respond immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic having cited the authority, you would need an opportunity to yourselves to consider it and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Bjelosevic. Before Ms. Korner resumes her cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I'm going to return to the prison book in a moment. But there is one other document that I should have asked you about in relation to Mr. Jorgic yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, 65 ter 20026, which is at tab 77. No. That's definitely not right [Microphone not activated] ... I see the B/C/S is not right, clearly. The English is right, but not the B/C/S, I don't think. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, and I'm afraid I haven't got any page numbers because we haven't got yesterday's transcript, that Mr. Jorgic had appeared from somewhere and was a member of the reserve police. In November, you -- you wrote to the ministry with completed forms of the individual IL-P and IL-R sheets. What are IL-P and IL-R sheets?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: IL-P means individual sheet of the dead, of those killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so IL --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: LP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And IL-R is wounded, is it, then?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is number 8 on that list the same Nikola Jorgic that we saw in that video yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The last name is the same, however, look at this: Jorgic, Stefan's son, Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Could you look at number 8, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, 8, sorry. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Jorgic, despite what he had been doing, despite his activities, was retained by you in the police, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by me, Mrs. Prosecutor. He was at the public security station for a while in the capacity of volunteers who were admitted into public security stations pursuant to that dispatch that we discussed which came from Mr. Pusina and Mr. Jasarevic. It was in keeping with that document that they would admit men into the station when choosing who was to be part of the police force, in addition to those who went through the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's take this in stages. You received this dispatch in April from Mr. Jasarevic, about which you've complained and which we've been through. By May the 3rd, you had taken the view, as I understood it, that there was no point in further communications because you couldn't communicate with the old BiH authorities and the CSB and the SJB in Doboj had been taken over by the Serbs. That's what you told us yesterday. Do you agree? Can you just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't be a full answer if I just said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly yes; partly no. Can I explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No because unless you say that my summary is in error in some way, then can we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You tell me where I've made an error in my summary of what you told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be easier that the witness explains. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm inviting -- I'm not inviting you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm inviting the witness to tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that when the communications were down, we weren't able to communicate with the old BiH authorities. Well, we weren't able to communicate with anyone because the communication lines were severed and we had no contact either with the former SRBiH organs or with the organs of the Serbian Republic of BiH. As of the 3rd of May, the CSB did not exist, as I put it. And, as you put it, you said that both these organisational units were not working. That's why I had to make this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand entirely what you're saying, that the CSB, for the reasons you've given, did not operate. But nonetheless, whether operating or not, from the 3rd of May onwards the SJB and the CSB were part of the Serbian MUP, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, yes. But some of it was operational and some of it wasn't. That's the key difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Mr. Jasarevic's illegal order, which you have said was illegal, from the 3rd of May onwards had absolutely no effect, did it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was created was a certain state of affairs which I repeatedly claimed was unlawful, and I stated the reasons. TO could only have been engaged as assistants to the police in situations where public law and order was seriously disrupted. But this was the situation that had been taken over from before, where some of the stations would obey the orders coming from Mr. Pusina and Mr. Jasarevic, and that was the head count that they had already had. And I can't even call the force that they had the police force, in proper terms. What else would happen? When an order would arrive that the MUP forces should be deployed to the front, the commander and the chief would, together, establish who was to be dispatched. They would draw up a list, and deploy them. On their return, they would produce an analysis of what had happened and would send a report to me that such and such a number of individuals were wounded or killed on such and such a day. And that's a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I suggest you're trying to sidetrack everybody from the original question that I'm asking you. Why, when you returned, as you say you did, at the beginning of July to the Doboj CSB, and after the 11th of July when all the question of these criminals who were in the police was discussed, why didn't you make it one of your first tasks to get rid of the murdering thugs who were part of the police?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who's to say we didn't? And I'm specifically referring to what the minister was asked to do and what I asked that be done out in the field. If you want to, we can go back to some of the notes from the meetings with chiefs of stations when such requests were made, on how many occasions, and what sort of information they reported back to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You knew --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can take it by individual dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. Bjelosevic. As I say, I suggest you're trying to sidetrack everybody, and me in particular. Why didn't you, knowing, as you did, that Jorgic was a murdering thug, why didn't you insist to your chief, Mr. Petricevic, that this man should be thrown out, and as Mr. Stanisic, in his order, said, suspended, pending criminal proceedings, and put at the disposal of the army. Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take it one by one. I'm truly not sidetracking you. I'm trying to elucidate things. I'm not shying away from anything. It was requested on several occasions verbally and in writing that the matters regarding to the force be sorted out. But let me tell you what the reality was and how things worked. A chief, not even today, would not have an insight into who happens to be where at what point of time. And let me speak in the first person, just as it was. If a chief of a station tells me at a meeting that the purging of the ranks, if you will, is ongoing, and then at the next meeting he tells me that it's all been sorted out, what was there for me to do? And later on - let me remind you of one event where notes were made as a result of one of these supervisory inspections, and I think it was Rajko Bilic who produced that report, where he, as an inspector, would make a fact-finding mission, not me, and then he would find that among the members of the reserve police there were such individuals who had criminal records and were prone to criminal conduct. But what was there for me to do? And I've stated this on a couple of occasions. When I spoke on this subject with the then chief of station Petrovic, he said that he was busy implementing this task but that he was fearful of these individuals. He tried to approach the matter with caution. As for suspensions, suspensions and disciplinary proceedings related only to the active-duty police force, not the reserve force, the reserve force would originate from the documents that were wartime assignments. I don't know if I've managed to explain clearly how things worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The reason for this notification to the MUP, I take it, with these forms was so that the named police officers could receive the appropriate benefits.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view of it was that we were given information. Now, to what end the information was used by those who received them, I don't know. But the information that we received from the ground, from public security stations, were processed and forwarded to the MUP, and that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So do we take it that in November, when you wrote this, Mr. Jorgic was still a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that he was there by that time. But look at the period; it was the 9th of August that he was wounded. I don't know where he was, but apparently he was out somewhere at the front line and wounded, as a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, isn't it the fact that you, Mr. Bjelosevic, and not only you, but I suggest your senior officers, superiors, were perfectly happy for the purposes of defeating, as you saw it, the enemy, to put these people into uniform and let them stay in uniform. That's the reality, isn't it? You made no effort because you were using these people.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I think that you are crystal clear on everything that I said. You've been dealing with this matter for a long time and you know that what I'm saying is absolutely true. You evidently have reasons for trying to deny it. Secondly, my position vis-à-vis the police and their moral integrity was clear and has not changed over the years. If you think that it was quite the opposite, then why don't you point me to a specific example where my conduct proves what you're saying? And the same goes for the then minister, Mr. Stanisic; I claim that his position was quite specific and clear. And anyone who intends to make a serious analysis of this, I would like to say that there is a number of documents confirming what I say, starting from the Belgrade meeting, to the notes made at the meeting, to a number of orders that followed the meeting where we established the MUP out in the field, in keeping with the law, to a number of reports coming from stations as to how this was done, to the various statements made at meetings. For instance, the meetings I held with chiefs of stations, where - and we can find specifically which meetings these were - when chief of the Doboj station Petrovic said the crime service has started making a record of crime. Does this say nothing to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask that this document be marked and admitted. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is again the same objection, Your Honour. I would -- I would suggest that we mark the document for identification, pending the -- the argument that we are going to -- to present to Your Honours about the -- the authority that I just cited at the beginning of this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that's totally wrong. But, again, this is the problem: I don't want to waste time on it. Your Honours, this is not, in a sense, new evidence. It couldn't have been produced until this witness gave evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, insofar as the Chamber has before it for consideration the -- this issue and it has yet to decide on the relevance of the authority cited by Mr. Zecevic this morning, it seems that we have no other course than what he has suggested. We mark it identification pending the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, yes, Your Honours, I just don't want to get lost, and we'll have to come back to that when Your Honours have heard full argument.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P2326, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like to go back now, please, to the book we were looking at yesterday and the three people that you were able to identify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that is - just a moment - it is P -- no, it's not. Yes, it's P1315. At tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we dealt with yesterday the law which you agree was that no one could be held in detention unless -- certainly by the police for more than three days, and, otherwise, if they went to a judge for an order. And you agree with that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The procedure is clearly stipulated by law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to waste time taking you through each of the entries. And if what I put to you is wrong, I will be corrected by the other side. But if one went through the book, Mr. Bjelosevic, we would find that Mr. Jovo -- Jozo Mandic, who you agreed you knew to be the president of the HDZ, is shown as being taken in and out to the MUP for interview on no less than 15 separate occasions between the 7th of May and the 23rd of June. Would you describe that as normal?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it came to be that Jozo Mandic was in detention and on the basis of whose decision. I really don't know that. I do know, however, that when a person was detained, then if any of authorised officials, officials from the police, had the need to conduct an official interview, such a person had to submit an official request. It meant that the person who made the decision on the detention was the person that had to allow such interview. In this particular case, I don't know how it went. I don't even know how many times he was interviewed or by whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You found out, however, that he was in detention, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday you showed me the prison book and I simply saw that his name was recorded in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Forget about the prison book. Are you saying that when you returned from your sojourn with the military you didn't discover that Mr. Mandic had been held in custody since the 7th of -- 7th of May, I think. Yes, 7th. He's number 3 on the list, 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, we should go to -- I'm so sorry, we should have gone to the page. It's, in B/C/S, at second page. Your Honours, I say the English doesn't help very much because it just shows what happens to them and the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see there he's number 3 on the list, brought in to custody on the 7th of May. And just so that we understand what the entries are at the side, we've got -- I think somebody's been through it already, but we've got the date and time he's taken out and the time that he's returned. And does that show - just let's take that very first entry - that on the 7th of May he was taken out at 2100 and returned at 2200, and he was taken to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I'll go back to the original question I asked. Are you saying that when you returned to your police duties you did not discover that Mr. Mandic was and had been in custody since the 7th of May?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say "discovered." You are describing the situation as if I was involved in some sort of investigation, research, discovery. I was informed by chiefs of stations, and I was informed about some issues. I was not involved in any sort of discovery. I really don't know what you mean to say when you say that I discovered something or that I did not discover something. That's not how things were functioning at the time. My role was not the role of an inspector who goes around researching and discovering things. I was the chief of the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I expect, Ms. Korner, that we're dealing with a difference in -- a language problem here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I'm going to -- I'm going to rephrase the question. Sorry. On, off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Petrovic or any of the prison authorities, because you spoke to them, according to you, tell you that in custody since the 7th of May had been Mr. Jozo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that anybody told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I don't know why this one name should have been specially emphasised among many names. Why should I have been informed about this particular man?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, because he was head of the Croat political party in Doboj. For once I will answer you. Wasn't that an important position?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was an important political function.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's look at the next name. Mr. Grgic, who's number 12, in custody since the 8th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before we move on. Mr. Bjelosevic, you answered that you didn't discover, you weren't told, about Mr. - what's his name again? - Mandic. In general, did you learn about him? I don't want to know whether you were told or discovered during some investigation. I just want to know: Did you learn, did you know, that he was in custody at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During May and June, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And he was in custody until when? Ms. Korner? I don't have it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll -- we're going to come to that. He was actually in custody until September when, as you'll see, he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Grgic, who you knew because he was the commander of the police station, wasn't he, before the war? A Croat.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He was actually retired at this time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The book shows -- and, again, as I say, I'm open to any corrections, that he was taken in and out for interview to the MUP, and once to hospital. In fact, there are a number of entries - perhaps we better have a look at that - for people being taken to hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look at page 6 and - 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 - 7. No. One more page then, please. It must be page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 16th of May, was he taken out from the MUP [sic]? And it looks like returned on the 19th. And was he in hospital? Is that what it shows?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner, you stated that he was taken to MUP and then hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I said hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was recorded on page 15, 22: "On the 16th of May, was he taken out from the MUP? And it looks like returned --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- oh, I'm sorry. From the MUP. From -- I'm sorry, from the prison. I beg your pardon. If I said from the MUP, I meant from the prison. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you know, don't you, that he was incredibly badly beaten up whilst he was being held in the prison?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that I don't know that. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but you sent, and we'll come on to that a little later because you've already looked at it. You sent this direction to your officers that -- that -- you know, that people were being badly beaten up in prison, because that's what you were being told. And he was one of them, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, did you say that I gave instructions that some of my people should go into the prison to beat up people? Did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you didn't. Never mind. Did you know that the ex-commander of the police station was badly beaten up?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to tell you what I found out about Karlo Grgic and how I found that out. May I say that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first part of my testimony, if you remember, I said that once I was called through the radio communications to go to Dragalic. That's where the place where exchanges were conducted. It's close to Okucani. I went there. I met Karlo Grgic's brother there. He was a policeman in Derventa. I used to know him. That's when he asked me about his brother. When I returned to Doboj, I inquired about Karlo Grgic and that's what I was told. This is what I was told: that he was detained, that he was interrogated, that he was taken to the hospital because, as I was told, he had been operated on sometime previously. I was told that he was hospitalised at the surgical department of the Doboj hospital, that one of the nurses brought his clothes and that he left the hospital. And the official version was that he set out towards Prisade, towards what was at the time called Usora municipality. And that is the information that I then sent to Marijan Grgic, Karlo's brother. So this is what I knew at the time. Now, as for when he was detained and whether I knew that he was detained when he was detained, well, I'm trying to convince you that I did not know that. I assure you that I did not know that. I told you what I knew. Much later I heard many other stories, other information, that he was killed, that he had escaped. But rumours is one thing and verified information is another. I really am not aware of the details. So this is how I gathered information about him, and I did it because his brother asked me to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you spoken to by Predrag Radulovic about Karlo Grgic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predrag Radulovic. I don't know whether I met Predrag Radulovic during the war --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... when you say --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I interrupted you. Go on. You did meet him because you met him in Teslic if nowhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what the witness said and you interrupted him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Well, he said -- I thought he said, I didn't meet him during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "Until ..." and then you interrupted him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, my fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After that, the incident in Teslic beginning of July, did he speak to you about Mr. Grgic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the incident in Teslic, I never spoke to Radulovic. Not for one or two months, but we didn't speak for several years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was really angry at that man. We never spoke. It took quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we take it that Mr. Radulovic, you say, never spoke to you about Karlo Grgic and that you said to him and complained that all these police officers, all these people, were being killed. And you said to him you could do nothing about it. That never happened. No conversation like that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you once again. After what happened in June in Teslic, after that meeting, the two of us did not speak for a long time. Later on, we discussed a number of topics, and it is possible that later on we also discussed some of the events dating from the war. And it is possible that our conversation may have touched upon that subject, but that was after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you, you see, Mr. Grgic disappears from the prison, or from the hospital, on the 24th of May, but at some stage during this period - not after the war - Mr. Radulovic spoke to you about Mr. Grgic. We've already dealt with that. All right. Finally, can we deal, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. But can the witness be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, he's already said it never happened. And I'm putting the Prosecution case on this. Well, he can certainly answer it again if you want him to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you're putting something to him, you should give him the opportunity to answer, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we're just wondering if you have brought any evidence to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- sustain your --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- point that there was such a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm reading from the transcript page 10800 to 10802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's my suggestion, Mr. Bjelosevic. That you did meet. That you did meet Mr. Radulovic, who spoke to you about the death of Mr. Grgic because it was a well-known notorious fact, and this was before the incident involving the Mice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if you want to say something like that, I would like you to tell me where it was and when it was that we met and had this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was in -- sorry. I can't give you an exact date. I can put to you that it was before the Mice incident and it was in your office.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No way. In my office? Mr. Radulovic definitely did not come to my office during that period of time. Something like that I certainly would have remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you should read from the part of the transcript what you just said because this witness that talks about that says on the same day. So, therefore, it is probably -- the day is probably identified. So -- so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because he says, On the same day, I met Andrija Bjelosevic. And therefore you should put to the witness exactly what the -- what the -- the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [Microphone not activated] ... I'm looking. I'm looking, Mr. -- all right. Can we -- can we go back ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... On the excerpt -- sorry. This on/off business is driving me bananas. The -- on the excerpt I have, there is no reference to what day it was. But we'll go back and see if we can find ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It refers, I believe, on page, if I may be of assistance, 10798 the report dated 17th of May, 1992, was discussed, and then it goes, Mr. Radulovic explains about --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, yes. I'm sorry, one of the rules is that you -- we shouldn't be doing it like this. I'm putting the suggestion, I've been asked what I base it on, I've given the answer to that. I will see if we can put a time and I'll come back to it, but I'd like to move on because this is just time-wasting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we -- Mr. Tipura who - if we go back, please, to the second page of the book - he, again, was an ex-police officer, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It we went -- he, too, was first arrested on the 7th of May. He was taken out to the MUP on eight occasions. And he died, didn't he, of his injuries in hospital in Banja Luka in September?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Tipura was more than just a policeman. Ilija Tipura had a Ph.D., and he was a dignitary. I heard what you just said, that he died in the Banja Luka hospital, but I don't know why he died there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would just like to say what my view is on that. Whoever brought in, questioned, detained Ilija Tipura, and especially if this, what you said, happened, that person made a bad mistake. On the basis of what I know about the man, Tipura.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you telling the Court that you didn't know that he was beaten up as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said what I thought and what I know. I say once again: Whoever did that made a terrible, terrible mistake. If he mistreated persons anyway. But especially not in this case, a person who most definitely did not deserve to be treated that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that's an answer, but I've been told off for pursuing matters, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This time you should insist, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bjelosevic, did you know - that was the question - did you know that he was beaten up or did you not know that he was beaten up? That has nothing to do whether you knew why he died. Did you know that he was beaten up or didn't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At the time, I most certainly did not know that Dr. Tipura had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now let's move back, please, to Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up on the screen, please, 20138, at tab 118. It was added last night, Your Honour, because we hadn't got a translation earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one intervention in the transcript, Your Honours. 22, page 22, 6, 7, and 8, I don't think the second -- the second sentence is -- is recorded properly. That is not what the witness said. So if this can be clarified with the witness. I'm sorry. I'm really not trying, but this would appear that -- that -- that the witness is actually agreeing with the mistreatment of, and instead he said something very -- totally different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. Do you mean the sentence, "If he mistreated persons anyway ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's obviously not what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I better correct this, although I think it's clear from your evidence what you were saying. "I have said what I thought and what I know. I say once again: Whoever did that made a terrible, terrible mistake." And you're then recorded as saying: "If he mistreated persons anyway. But especially not in this case ..." I think what you were saying was if persons were mistreated, if, in the -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that whoever did that, if that person did that kind of thing anyway, that kind of mistreatment, I'm saying that mistreating people generally is a bad mistake. And in this particular case, if this happened to Dr. Tipura. It should never happen. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go back then, please, to the document that's now up on the screen. This is a criminal report dated the 10th of August, 1992, against a number of different people with number one as Jozo Mandic, born 9th of September, 1921. So in 1992 he was 69 years -- sorry, 71 years old. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is information about his date of birth, yes. He was born in 1921.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You knew him to be -- you knew him personally, didn't you, Mr. Bjelosevic? He was an old man.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him at two meetings, I think, in the Autumn of 1991, at a meeting that I had initiated. I asked Mr. Alicic to convene a meeting after what happened in Brod. I asked him to host the meeting, and I asked that all relevant persons be invited so that we can discuss that subject in order to have everyone work in a calming fashion. I remember that he was at that meeting then, and I may have seen him another time. I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to the last page, please, just to see who signed this. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So by the 10th of August, 1992, at the very latest, you knew that Mr. Mandic was in custody, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I have to know that he was in custody? I would most kindly ask you to go back to the first page so that it would be easier for me to give an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go -- sorry, can we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please look at the top of the page. You see it says National Security. If that service processed information about certain individuals and if they said that on the basis of their information, when they established the facts, et cetera, if they write up a criminal report, I had to trust them. Not going individually by name into who was where at the time. However, I believed them, if they wrote this up, and if they are invoking -- look at all the articles here - look at this. Pursuant to Article so on and so forth. I believed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question was whether you knew in August, when you signed this criminal report, the -- security services -- the National Security Service, the SNB having conducted an investigation, that he was in custody?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given you an answer to that question. I didn't know who was where at that point in time, because I signed a report that they had processed and prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, there was a part of a question that Ms. Korner had asked earlier which, implicitly, I thought you had adopted: Did you know Mr. Mandic beforehand, before this -- the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I think not. I think I did not know that he was in custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, no. That isn't my question. My question is whether you knew him. I have a follow-up question, but the -- but what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. Yes, I've already answered that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So my question is: Although you didn't, yourself, prepare this report, it was prepared by whatever the working system was that you have and you signed off on it, did the -- did it strike you that among the persons listed was Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a long time ago, and I cannot speak about it in great detail now. However, I will tell you one thing. Irrespective of someone's important political office, that was not a reason for that person not to do something that was against the law, to do something wrong. And I would certainly not be the person to say, Wait a moment, he's the president of a political party, or to amnesty anyone in any way. If the service wrote up something, I would have to have strong indicia, to the effect that something was wrong, to ask for something to be revised, to put a question mark, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I wasn't going so far, Mr. Bjelosevic. My question was merely: Having regard to the fact that you knew Mr. Mandic beforehand, and knew something about him, whether, at the time you signed this report, it is something that, as it were, stood out? That's the only question I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I do not recall. The signature is placed on the last page. After all these years, it is hard for me to remember with reliability whether I looked through all the names. I don't know even know if I looked through all the names, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the last page, please, and we'll see the answer to the question. Just above the list of the names, do you see the words in the paragraph that begins, "We remark that the charged Mandic," et cetera, "are in detention at the regional prison Doboj"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't relevant for me either, in terms of whether I should sign the criminal report or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It didn't cross your mind that perhaps it wasn't a terribly good idea that a 71-year-old man should have been in prison from May through to when you signed this report in August?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for police custody, it is decided upon by the person who was in charge of the case up until then. After the time provided for by the law for police custody, after that expires, then I could not decide about it any longer. So I didn't even go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He and all the other people named were allegedly having committed the offence of armed rebellion against the Serbian state. That's right, isn't it? If you go back -- we'll go back to page 1 -- page 2, sorry, the end of the list.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is probably as is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If true - leaving aside the legal technicalities of how you were rebelling against the Serbian state before it came into existence; that's not the point, but - it is an extremely serious offence. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is how the law treated it at that time. Who took part in the creation of paramilitary formations and their arming and took part in armed activity was thereby committing a crime. That is what the law said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's look at what happened, please, to Mr. Mandic. Could we have up, please, the video which is at 20135, and the transcript is at tab 116. The part is at -- starts at 53 minutes -- the part that we're going to see starts at 53 minutes in, and the transcript part is at page 19 of the document. And we need sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The petrol station in Dragalic not far from Nova Gradiska has become a place of freedom for another couple of hundred prisoners from Bosnia and Herzegovina." "I find it difficult to talk. I can't talk." "Reporter: What is the situation like in Doboj?" "Mandic: Very bad. I spent 125 days in prison. From the first day. It's hard, I can't talk." "What did they do there?" "Mandic: I will tell journalists ... when I get to Kljujic, Mesic and Perica. In the last minute, from the prison onto a bus. I left two apartments, two houses, a car, 150 "dulums" of land ... from the time the main committee was organised in Sarajevo and Doboj, for Doboj municipality, I worked fair and square ..." "Reporter: Did you come directly from prison?" "Yes, directly from prison. There was an exchange because probably Mesic or someone ... They arrested everyone ... on the street ... at their houses. I was captured the first day. They searched my house and took everything. I had a pension. I retired 12 years ago. They seized my two apartments, two houses, 150 "dulums" of land, a car. Fortunately, my son somehow managed to leave. He immediately left for Slovenia with his wife and three children. He is an engineer. But everyone has to move out." "What is the situation like in occupied Doboj?" "Very bad. Very bad. Very bad. This is a tragedy." "How many Croats and Muslims remained there?" "I don't know exactly, but very few. Many Muslims have fled to Tesanj. Women, children, and men. The remainder stayed in town, but even they want to leave. There are many here in these three buses. And Muslims." "How long were you there?" "I spent 125 days in prison from the first day, from the 3rd of May. There were two detention camps - one in Usora and one in the barracks in Pare where a tank unit had been located. Perhaps about 4.000 people were detained. I lost a lot of weight. Do you see the holes in my belt? For 40 days I ate only two meals a day - 100 grams of bread and some water. Nothing else. So I ..." "How old are you?" "I'm 72 years old ... but I was in good shape ... detention crushed me. I was beaten ... There was much beating there ... by the army, police. I was badly beaten too. No questions were asked. Soldiers and policemen in transit. There are fire or six kinds of troops - Arkan's Men Chetniks, and those with hats, the men from Knin, and people are completely -- well, lately, when UNPROFOR apparently started intervening, but they could not intervene in the prison. I managed to do a little something but through a lawyer, but now ..." "Just tell us your name, in the end." Answer: "I am engineer Jozo Mandic. I am from Doboj. I lived there for 45 years. I worked for 40 years for the railways. I was retired, and then as a retired person I was elected president of the HDZ in Doboj municipality and participated in all the forums, but in a fair and honourable way. I think ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This exchange of a man you had signed a report for saying that there was evidence he was guilty of armed rebellion, were you present? Because it was apparently at the petrol station in Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragalic was a place where exchanges happened anyway. And I said that I was there only once. It wasn't this particular time. It was before that. As I watch this video, it takes me back to the time. Unfortunately, this is one of the thousands of stories of people from all sides. You heard that it was an exchange. You could see that on the other side too. I'm not underestimating anyone's suffering or sacrifice, and I'm not justifying anyone's crime by somebody else's crime. But what I wish to point out is that this is one of the many stories, destinies, of one particular individuals [as interpreted] within everything that had happened in the area. Believe me, you could have heard thousands of stories like this, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in light of the legal matters we discussed, may I ask that it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that portion will be Exhibit P2327, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that only that portion, of what is a lengthy video, is going to become the exhibit. And, if necessary, we'll put it onto a separate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you remind me the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, the tab number is 116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And this is a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zecevic asked if we could give -- put a date when the meeting with Mr. Radulovic took place. We've checked the previous transcript pages, and I'm open to any corrections that Mr. Zecevic wishes to make, all we can seem to be able to say is that at that stage the discussion -- at an earlier stage, I'm sorry, there was a discussion of a document dated the 17th of May, 1992. The questions then continued, and all we can say is it appears to have been an occasion sometime between the -- well, it has to have been the 25th May, because that's the last entry in the prison record for Mr. Grgic, and obviously the 30th of June. So that's the best we can do. If Mr. Zecevic thinks that there's any better we can do, then I'm open to suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you want me to talk about that in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... all right, well that's -- in which case -- well, I don't want -- again, this is my problem. I don't want to waste time. Is it something, perhaps, we can discuss at the next break and see if we can get something better?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you now, on the -- still on the topic of this prison and what was happening, for you to have another look at this document that you told us about when you were giving evidence in chief. And it is tab 25 in our bundle. It's P1305, and there's also -- it was in the Defence bundle, as well, as tab 49. It's the one I'm sure you remember because you said that you found that a knife had been stuck through it. It's the order that you made on the 12th of June. And this is what you said about it when you were giving evidence in chief at page 19628: "This is a document that I signed and I dictated so that it be typed up. And it was done in quite a bit of a hurry, as I was coming to the centre. It was either the prison warden or the deputy that I came across, and this person told me that they had certain problems regarding the entry of different persons wearing different uniforms, that they would violently enter the premises of the prison, and that they committed violent acts against the prisoners there, and the prison asked for help." Now, by the 12th of June, therefore, Mr. Bjelosevic, you were aware that people were going into the prison and beating up prisoners there; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can. As I said, I received the information from either the warden or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But can we just look at the first three lines of this order: "I strictly prohibit arbitrary entry into the premises of the Dobrinja District Prison rooms for temporary detention of persons in public security stations ..." So we take it from that this is an order directed to your police, that you knew also on the 12th of June that people were being detained in the SUP -- the SJB, I should say.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the public security stations had a room set aside for persons who were taken into custody but were not officially detained. There were a number of reasons for which persons could be taken into custody. They could be intoxicated and disrupt public law and order and would be kept in that room until they sobered up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But, I'm sorry, you're prohibiting people coming into the rooms for temporary detention of persons in public security stations. Can we take it from that, Mr. Bjelosevic, that you were aware that people were beating up detainees in the police stations as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then: "... as well as the use of physical intimidation and physical force against imprisoned and detained persons." Now, did you, yourself, when you got this information that people were being beaten up in the police stations, instigate immediately an investigation into how that was happening?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you put it, only I would have sufficed there, and I should have been everywhere, seen everything, and taken decisions about everything. So I didn't need inspectors, chiefs of stations, commanders, or police officers themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the moment, you said that you were engaged on the military duties during this period. But didn't you think this was an important enough occasion to call together the chiefs of, at the very least, Doboj, and Samac, or the commanders, to say, "I want an immediate investigation in what is going on in the beating of prisoners"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see, it's the 12th of June. I was certainly not able to invite Samac because there was no communication between Samac and Doboj, as the corridor had not yet been opened. On this date, the activities aimed at opening up the corridor were at their most intense. And what I was able to do on the fly, as it were, during my brief visits there was the best I could do. In my evidence so far, I said that perhaps it wasn't up to speed in terms of how the situation dictated it, but I did as best I could, and you saw how I faired after having written this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we've heard your account of what you say happened. Were you yourself ever present in the building, because it -- the building contained the SJB and CSB offices, when people were being beaten up in that building?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned it that on one occasion as I entered the building I came across a number of people standing in the corridor who had been taken in. They held their hands against the wall and were singing songs. I was very much surprised by what I saw, and exclaimed, What's happening here? As I entered the room where duty police officers were located, I asked them what this was all about. As I spoke to them through an opening in the wall, there was a person coming down the corridor -- or, rather, there were two individuals coming down the corridor who held their chins high and said, It was us who brought them in. And I said, Well, on whose orders was this? And they haughtily said that they had arrested, as they put it, the Ustashas. I ordered my men to release these individuals and to throw the two men out of the station. And that's how it happened. The two armed men left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for the chief at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really am going to stop you there because you did talk about this before. But my question, which I will say again, was: Were you present when people were being beaten up? Not singing songs.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone being beaten up in the corridor as I got in. But I did see individuals as they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I think the answer to my question is, no, you didn't see them being beaten up. Did you see people in the SUP -- or, I'm sorry - the SUP -- in the building with obvious signs of injury?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well -- all right.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever hear screams coming from the prison which was next door to the building from the people who were being - and I use the word "tortured" - there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to have a look, please, at a document for a moment. Another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have, please, on the screen document 20133, tab 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask what is the provenance of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's an article published in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the Internet?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not proposing to exhibit it. I want to ask one question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just note it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, I don't know if it is on the -- I mean, that's where it's been got from, but I think it's actually published in something called BIRN, B-I-R-N.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This was an article, a very recent one, on the 18th of November last year largely dealing with what happened in Doboj and the evidence of Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could with go, please, in English to the third page. And I think it's all in one page in B/C/S. No, it's not, sorry. Second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I would suggest, Ms. Korner, just for the consistency of the -- of the presentation of evidence in this case, I suggest you pose the question. You don't need the document. Because I can -- I can possibly list a number of occasions where you yourself and the other members of the Office of the Prosecutor were complaining about the documents coming from the Internet, and there has been some rulings from the Trial Chamber in that -- in this respect. Perhaps the best way to proceed would be that you ask the question. You don't need this document, because you cannot show us the provenance of this document. It's obviously taken from the Internet. We don't know who wrote it or anything else for that matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, aren't you anticipating the -- we don't know what the question is. And the issue of provenance is something that we need only exercise our minds about if there were attempts to exhibit it. Isn't that where we are?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but the problem is that it is my understanding that Ms. Korner was asking for the third page. I assume she is going to read from the document, and that is the anticipation, and my objection was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I would have thought -- well, I shouldn't say -- I thought that the way that we dealt with documents such as this is that before counsel asking the question phrases it, that the witness is invited to look at the document and then the question is asked. So we avoid the -- any suggestion of the document being sneaked into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's completely different because we do know the provenance and can, if required, prove the provenance. The objections earlier have been to documents that suddenly appear on General Praljak's web site.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you contacted, Mr. Bjelosevic, by reporters last year?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the telephone?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did they ask you about what Mr. Petrovic had said?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I forgot the reporter's name, but he said that he was an investigative journalist and asked me about some of the statements made by Obren Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. And did he put to you the statement made by Mr. Petrovic that you, your office was on the first floor of the CSB, could have heard the sounds of non-Serbs being beaten in the police station in Doboj, and did you reply, The essential issue is not whether this could be heard or not but why it could be heard, and then saying that you did not want to comment about the details? Did you give that reply?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the essential bit is not whether you heard sounds of somebody being beaten but why these individuals were being beaten. So that's what I said, not whether -- how far you could hear a person being tortured but why that person was tortured. That was the essential issue in my view. And that was the question put to me. And I do still think that this is the essential question to be put.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, effectively, you didn't answer the reporter's question. Because what he was putting to you, wasn't he, in effect, was whether you had heard people being beaten in the police building, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what the question was. He asked me if I was aware of the statement made by Obren Petrovic, who, in answer to what was probably a question from the prosecutor, on the issue of people being taken into custody and beaten, was supposed to answer the question of whether the sounds of beating could be heard as far as my office, and that was what I told him in this response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You never heard -- and you never heard anybody being beaten, any screams of people being beaten?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time when I was present in my office, I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admittedly, I spent very little time there. But when I was there, I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I want to move away now from the topic of prisons and prisoners and look at some of the people who were on the police payroll during the course of this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, first of all, at the document which I think you looked at before. It's P1346, tab 13.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the number of this tab?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's not. I think it was in the Defence binder, but I don't know what number it was. Oh, I'm told it wasn't. So you'll just have to look at it on the screen. Now, this is, which comes from the Doboj CSB, a -- what's called an advance payment payroll list for April of 1992. And in April 1992, you are still working, aren't you, in the CSB Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the Special Group Doboj that's having advance payment here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. It's the month of April, and I can see that it says that it's an advance payment of the salary for the month of April 1992. The signatures I see at the bottom are unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was it part of your duties from time to time, if not regularly, to check the payrolls?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To check them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. To check that -- that -- that, you know --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did sign some payrolls, but I am unfamiliar with this. I'm going through the names now and I recognise the first and the eleventh name. There is a total of 11 of them. And what surprises me is that Nenad Kujundzic was a police officer in the Doboj Public Security Station, in other words within our building. And to see this, together with the words "special group," is unfamiliar. I don't know who wrote this or signed it. But it could have something to do with the fact that some -- somehow that money had to be accounted for. It was through the months of August and September that we had to deal with the funds arriving from the SDK and the bank and a certain amount from the post office as well -- or, rather, these funds having been lost somewhere, we didn't know what had become of the money and we were trying to track it down. So this may have been a part of it. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can we stop there, please, because you say the security services station. This is the Security Services Centre. This is not the SJB; this is the CSB Doboj, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely why I was telling you this, if you had been listening carefully. What I was surprised by was that the document is not dated. The only reference to time we have is the month of April. Second of all, I said that Nenad Kujundzic was a police officer in the SJB Doboj in April and there was no special group or special unit within the centre. Besides, I don't know these other individuals or their names, if that's the Nenad I'm referring to. And I know the name of Radojica Bozovic, but to my knowledge he was not there in April. I don't know what this document is or what it represents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to make out the text on the seal as well, but it's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... yes, this man -- thank you. We saw the name of this man Bozojovic [phoen] yesterday in the report by Milos, didn't we? That the activities of him and his men were causing outrage - I'm summarizing, and I don't know if anybody wants to -- amongst the citizens of Doboj. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, the name I received in interpretation was Zojovic. Is that a new name?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The man we can see on the first -- as number one on this list of the Special Group Doboj.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Bozovic. Not Zojovic. I received it as Zojovic in interpretation; that's what confused me. So I suppose that's the same name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And weren't you --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't have any information that this man was in Doboj in the month of April. And I particularly don't have any information about him being in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question should be put to the author of the document. I don't know anything about it, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that somebody in your centre - and it's stamped and signed - without your knowledge was authorising payment for a group of people headed by this man called Bozovic, entitling it "Special Group Doboj," without any input or knowledge by you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know absolutely anything about the document. The author, the date on which it was made, I don't recognise the signatures or the seal. Nothing. The only thing I could assist you with is with those two names that I recognise, and at least they have the same first and second name of the individuals I know. But as for the rest of the document, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But all these documents which are maintained - and maintained still at Doboj - were open for inspection by inspectors from the MUP, by yourself, by anybody, weren't they, who had lawful authority to look at these documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this may assist, I can ask to be granted access, when I go back, and try and find out at least something about the document, which I can then relate to you over the phone or via the videolink or in some other way. If you think that can help, I will do my best to see if the documents are still there and, if so, to see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can assure you the document is still there, because we acquired it, Mr. Bjelosevic. It's one of the financial documents remained. Anyhow, I've dealt with that. You don't know who this man is other than, as you told us yesterday, he had something to do with the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which man?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yesterday, when I showed the report -- we can have it up again if you want because we've looked this up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up document, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just tell me the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The number one on your list. The name I have such difficulty in pronouncing.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozovic. Yes, we discussed him yesterday. And I told you what I know about that man.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So you had no idea until I showed you this document, is that what you're saying, that this man was actually being paid as a policeman? Is that what you're telling me -- or telling the Court, rather.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly you said. I received somewhat complicated interpretation of your words. Yesterday we talked about it. And yesterday I said something about Bozovic. And today I said, and I'm going to repeat it once again, that in April there was no special group attached to the CSB, and I'm not aware that those monies were paid for this period, and I don't know who wrote this document. And I am saying it once again: If the Chamber deems it necessary I can, upon my return, try to figure out what is it -- what this is all about. I can really try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My question is: Before you saw this document, is it your contention that you did not know that number one on this list, Mr. Bozovic, was, on the face of it, in any event, a police officer?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him as Major Bozovic. I was told that he was a major.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move to the next document, please, which is -- oh, I'm sorry. Your Honours, is this an exhibit? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. Thank you. Could I -- could we look next, please, at 20113, tab 26B of our documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I find it in this binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Then I will look at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is a document of actual payment, it looks like, because it's got signatures. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to the sixth page, please, in B/C/S. And it's the fifth in -- in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there a signature there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the signature of Obren Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go back, please, to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is payment for the Special Unit Doboj. What was the Special Unit Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's something -- probably something that was in the station. There is a document drafted by the chief of the station in relation to obtaining supplies for the public security station, and this document also stipulates who was in charge of that for the police. And the special police is mentioned there. Nenad Kujundzic was in charge of it, so I assume that this is a matter that you should clear with Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no. Let's take this in stages, sir. This is clearly a relatively large unit of -- special police unit, 50 men, if we -- sorry, I suppose we better go to the --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I can see 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Let's go --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the third page, please, in each.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We see 50 people all together listed. I have skipped one of the pages. Now, wasn't this the equivalent of the Banja Luka Special Police. This was the Doboj equivalent, Mr. Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what else was it? I mean, this is clearly something that existed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm doing my best. Now I see the signature at the bottom on the left, which I cannot recognise. And the front page -- can I take a look at the front page once again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I was going to go back to the front page in any event. Yes, you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to see once again what's written here, because I'm doing my best to explain it. So it says Special Unit Doboj above organisational unit, 18th of June. I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's take number one on the list. You know exactly who Mr. Karagic is, don't you, because you spoke about him last time or when you were giving evidence in answer to questions by Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. But there's no signature confirming that he received the money. Have you noticed that? I don't know what this is. And I see that there are some other names listed here without the signature that they've actually took the money. Take a look at number 19, Starcevic, and also on the following pages.
