So I really don't know what this is about. But if you're asking me who Slobodan Karagic, that I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you've told him about him. And you had dealings with Mr. Karagic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I was summoned to a court in a case against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, but you knew --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. Hang on. You knew who he was, didn't you, in 1992, not just when you were summoned to court as a witness. I want to come back to that later. You knew exactly who Mr. Karagic was, didn't you, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, I knew it. I knew it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Karagic - I'm calling him Mr. Karagic - like the man we looked at -- yes -- no. Well, like Bozovic and yesterday's man -- Jorgic - thank you, Your Honour - was another murdering thug, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he was a murder. Let me just tell you one thing. Up until the beginning of the war, I hadn't [Realtime transcript read in error "had"] been living for very long time in Doboj. I suppose it's a sort of handicap for me, the fact that I didn't know the people well. I began working in Doboj at the beginning of May 1991, and I came to live there sometime in November. However, I know that he was a taxi driver and that he was a rather problematic character.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that hides a multitude of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There is one intervention in the transcript. 48, 3, the witness says very short time in Doboj, not very long time in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, problematic hides a multitude of sins, Mr. Bjelosevic. Let's not beat about the bush. He was a well-known criminal, wasn't he, in the Doboj area?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well ... my information about that person is as follows: He was a taxi. He smuggled foreign currency before the war. Maybe this is not really a proper way of saying things about him in public, but that's what I know about him. I don't know that he was a murder. I am aware of a story about some activities of his - how should I put it? - rather cruel activities directed at certain persons at the beginning of the war. I also known that currently he is serving sentence for a criminal offence in the nature of robbery. And if I remember it well, the person who had been robbed was also wounded with a knife. And I think that he is currently serving the sentence for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're absolutely right about that, Mr. Bjelosevic. Finally, to move on, are you telling the Court, again, that you had no idea that Mr. Karagic was on the police payroll?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karagic was in the military for a while, and he spent some time in the reserve police force. I cannot tell you the exact dates, but he was part of both structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again, a part of witness's answer was not recorded and it might be important. 49, 4, the witness named the -- the institution where the -- Mr. Karagic was in the reserve police force, and I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you heard that, Mr. Bjelosevic. Did you name where he was?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that he was in the reserve police force in the police station in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And let's now look, please, at a payroll for the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honours, that one's not an exhibit. May I ask that that be -- that one, can I say straightaway, we acquired something like last week. But, Your Honours, given that you say that everything should be marked for identification, can we have this one marked for identification as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, marked for identification, yes. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So entered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P2328, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now could you look, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up on the screen, I should say, document which is P1338. Oh, tab 14F. All right. Could we go to the next page, please, in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an advance -- sorry. Yes, a list of employees to receive an advance salary, CSB Doboj. It's stamped; is that correct? Do you recognise the stamp there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that -- that's the Doboj stamp, is it? The official Doboj stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, if we can just specify which of -- because there are two stamps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Certainly. Let's take the large stamp first. Let's enlarge it, shall we? Can we see if we can get just the bottom bit. Yep.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think this is going to help to explain some things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask questions, then you can give me an explanation, if you want. Is that -- please, is that large stamp the official Doboj stamp?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it remains to be seen when it was legally valid. This confirms what I was explaining earlier. The lists were made retroactively. There are several reasons for that. If you want me, I can explain for every individual on the list who he or she is and why the name is on the list. If that's important. If not, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can in a moment. I just want, please, to establish certain things about this document and then can you tell me what you want -- or you can tell the Court, rather. There's a smaller stamp next to that. What's that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me take a look. I cannot see what's written --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... over the top, there's a signature. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is my signature. But you asked me to identify the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Is that the sort of official Doboj stamp?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The big one, on the left, yes, it was the official stamp. But with all my effort I didn't manage to identify even the letters on the small stamp. I'm not sure whether it's Latinic or Cyrillic. If I knew the letters, then maybe I would be able to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the list and I will -- in one moment can you give me the explanation you want to. Does that show, as 1 and 2 yourself as the chief and Mr. Savic as the assistant chief?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Explain, please, as you wish to, why it is that Mr. Savic, who you say wasn't a proper police officer, wasn't appointed until the 23rd of June, is being paid for -- a salary for April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain it. You saw a number of documents which show that in April 1992 the centre worked with its full complement from before the war. And according to the rules, the salaries should have been paid by the Ministry of Interior of BiH. Due to wartime events and due to the fact that the communications were cut off, the salaries were not paid. These were not paid at all during a period of time. Subsequently, when some funds were acquired, it was decided to pay the salaries retroactively. Now, why did I state that it's a fortunate circumstance that we identified this stamp? This must have been done at least in July. Here you can see the names. Jovo Josipovic, that was a policeman in the traffic police station in Derventa. And I think that he arrived in Doboj sometime in May. Then Marija Cudic [phoen] was a technical secretary in the public security sector. So the lists were made retroactively. This fact is confirmed the new stamp which is in Cyrillic [as interpreted]. And another thing that I remember from 1992 is that the lists were made, some of them very orderly, some of them not so orderly, in order to justify the funds that were taken from the safe of the public accountancy service and from the bank. At the time, there was a huge inflation, daily inflation. So after a month, this money could have been devalued, I think I'm not going to exaggerate if I say 1000 times. So the nominal value in April, for instance, one dinar, it became 1000 times less valuable because of the inflation. So it was convenient to justify things with these kind of documents. You also could have seen from my notes that I wanted to explore this more thoroughly, and I don't know exactly how this story ended. As more Milan Savic, let me clarify one thing. I believe you are interested in this topic, so I would like to elucidate it. Milan Savic was the counter-sabotage technician. However, his wartime assignment was in a military unit. As far as I know, his military booklet is in Teslic. It was kept there, maybe even copied, and that's how it was established that he belonged to that unit. And he had to draw salary from somewhere. And since this was made sometime in July, the person who made this list simply wrote down that he was assistant commander, but we know, because we saw the decision, from which date on he was the assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's another piece of paper, I suggest, Mr. Bjelosevic, that has very little to do with the reality of matters. Why, hearing what you say, that this was done afterwards to get people paid, did you sign off for Mr. Savic to get paid as assistant chief in April, when you say he was no such thing?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His status in April was not as described here. But since the funds involved were so small, maybe this is going to sound incredible to you, but I think that speaking in today's money this may have been 3 or 4 euros. This was really done to satisfy the formalities and to define status-related issues. And as for that money's worth, it was really not significant at all. So really no -- nothing really was gained here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But according to you it's not until June that Mr. Savic ever becomes a properly paid-up member of the police force. Why did you agree for him not only to be paid wrongly, as assistant chief, but at all by the police, when you say he was in a military unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, do I understand the effect of your evidence to be - and these are my words, not -- I'm summarizing - that this is an entirely fictitious document created for audit purposes only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say that it was made for audit purposes only. I was talking about the fact that the monies were insignificant and that these payouts were more oriented towards the purpose of status-related issues such as pension, social security, numbers of years of service, and other things. Because, in parallel with these salaries, the contributions for social security and the pension funds were paid as well, and that was the main purpose. The amounts mentioned here today would not be more than 3 or 4 euros, so nothing would be gained from that. The main purpose were status-related issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, is that why on one of the other payrolls we saw, about the Doboj Special Unit, the amounts are, if I remember well, 80.000 dinar for one month? Or do I have that wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite understand, I'm sorry. It has to do with the previous list, does it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the first -- the first payroll you showed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The first one was the one with Bozovic on it. The second -- oh, sorry. The first one was Bozovic; the second one - I'll just need to get it out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can call the document so the witness can comment, because he doesn't have the documents with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. It's 20 ... it was 20113, which has now got a MFI number, but I can't remember what it was. 23 -- 2328. Yes, 60.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Hmm. Yes, there it is. 80.000, 60.000, 45.000, if I read that well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you please tell me what the question is now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My question is: Is the explanation you gave about inflation and -- and what -- what the 6.000 or the 4.500 on the other document means in real value? Is that the explanation why, here, a monthly salary seems to be 80.000 or 60.000 and not 6.000? I mean, that is a salary ten times more than the one that you received, if I go back to the other document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you that it all depends on when this was written. If you followed what I was saying, one question had to do with regulating status-related issues for employees. This was form rather than actual benefit. Secondly, as I have pointed out several times, there had to be justification for the money that went somewhere. Then lists were made retroactively and then it said that salaries were paid out to such and such and such a person. And given this staggering inflation, it was so convenient to justify it that way. May I tell you that for a long time everybody who lived in that part of the world knew that one's salary would amount to a few drinks, for example, and nothing more than that. In those days, a salary was symbolical basically, and it had to do with status-related issues. In these cases, it was also used to account for the money that someone had taken somewhere. To this day, I'm not sure whether light has been shed on that properly. And so on. I don't know how useful this has been and how useful my overall answer has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid not at all, Mr. Bjelosevic. I was just wondering why a salary of one policeman on one document is 60.000 and the salary of another policeman on another document, pertaining to the same month, is 6.000. I mean, that's a different you can't explain unless it would be the explanation of inflation, I don't know. I just -- I just try to understand what -- what was going on then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understood you better. It's not the same month. That was made for the month of April, so certain proportions were taken into account, and you see that this has to do with the month of May. Inflation was -- I don't know. I cannot go into the actual figures involved. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So this would be just the inflation -- the effect of the inflation in one month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Even on a daily basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd just like to go back to my original question, is: Why, for whatever purpose, you signed off a document that would give Mr. Savic a salary when he wasn't, according to you, even a member of the police in April, let alone assistant chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the reason why I had intervened, it was because of the question that you had asked. Because if, as I -- although the witness didn't accept my suggestion, if -- and in his later answer to Judge Delvoie -- the impression I had is that this was window dressing of some form or other. And I don't know that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, window dressing -- no, no, my -- well, we ought to confirm this with the witness. My understanding is they didn't get paid in April when they should have got paid in April. And so this was a retroactive method of achieving payment. That was my understanding of what the witness said. Not that this was simply a document put together for the purposes of accounting for money that had gone. He said they should have been paid by BiH; they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your question is specifically that among those who should have been paid, is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's exactly the point I'm trying to get across.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So what I'm trying to -- Mr. Bjelosevic, accepting, let's say, for the moment, what you say, that this was a back-dated document, why would you sign off on Mr. Savic getting paid for April when he had never been paid -- sorry, he had never, in April, been a member of the police, on your account?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously you have misunderstood some of the things I've said. I don't know who has the document, the copy of Milan Savic's military booklet. You will see there that already in 1991 he received his war assignment in that unit. If you look at the information bulletins, you will see that Milan Savic, as a technician for counter-sabotage protection, went to on-site investigations in 1991 and 1992. Now, what happened? His regular --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, I'm --

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- status --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no, I'm sorry. Again I'm going to stop this. Was he -- no, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, but, Ms. Korner, the witness gave the answer. I'm trying to find it because there is -- there is obviously a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... well, can I -- that's why I want to short-circuit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, but please ask the question -- I mean, clearly to the witness, because he already gave the answer and you missed the answer. And that is the problem which is confusing the witness and all of us, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a simple way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was -- in April, was Mr. Savic a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He never severed his employment with the MUP. If you want to be sure that what I'm say is correct, do ask the MUP of BH for lists. I think that they had received copies, and you will see that for January and February and March his salary had been paid out to him, but his military assignment was in that -- his war assignment was in that military unit. Perhaps you do not fully understand it, but that's the way things were. And then in April it went on. He did not ask for termination of employment. Disciplinary measures were not taken against him in the ministry. He was still an employee of the ministry. You will see, in April, from the bulletins and the rest, you will see that the man went to on-site investigations, that he was working as a technician.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's fine. That's absolutely fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just found the reference, so I can give you 53 -- page 53, 3 and 4, where he says Milan Savic was the counter-sabotage technician. And it is my understanding that he was employed by MUP at the time, as a counter-sabotage technician in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I'm prepared entirely to accept that -- that I thought he was referring to the military. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So he was working in the police, but he was not, you say, the assistant chief in April?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I want to ask you one last -- about one last name on this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said yes, I think, didn't you? He was working for the police but wasn't assistant chief; the answer to that is "yes"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One last question about a name -- it's a very lengthy document. It seems there were a lot of employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If it's a lengthy document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I only want to look at one name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then -- I know, Your Honours, we've gone a little past the break. Page 9 in English and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't want to confuse or anything, but can we -- we didn't get which document. You said page 9, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. We have to go back to the other. I had forgotten we'd gone into this document. All right. 13 -- 1338. Page 9 in English; page -- and 9 in B/C/S. Page 9 in B/C/S, please. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: April, signed off by you again, is it, Mr. Bjelosevic? Mr. Karagic. And as you point out, inflation was enormous because for April you're going back to 4.000.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said my signature?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the same exhibit, Your Honours. It's the whole -- the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... is that 14F --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tab 14, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] F?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 14F, which starts with the document with Mr. Bjelosevic or whatever, and it goes all the way through for about nine pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I cannot identify this signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You still say you didn't know that Mr. Karagic was being paid as a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that Karagic was in the military for a while and in the reserve police, milicija, for a while too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just checking. I don't think this one is an exhibit either. So could I have that, please, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, right. So it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honours, I have -- I have -- now I have a problem with this document. Because the first -- sorry, six or eight pages are the documents which have two stamps. And the last three are the documents which have -- the last three, yes, just have one stamp, the small stamp, and it's obvious that the signature is different, at least to me. Now, maybe after the break we can come back to this and discuss it a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I say, I don't know whether this is a question on the provenance, these -- we can actually call the witness who seized the documents from Doboj. So there is no problem about this. If there's a suggestion that these documents come from anywhere else, these were recovered from the Doboj CSB archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My problem is that this document is given one exhibit number, and it's obviously that it consists of two sets of different documents. That is my problem. And it's given one exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is misleading, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't know whether it's separate or not. If there's going to be a discussion about this, it's something to be adjourned. Is this the way in which it was put together as a document. You will see that it contains continuous ERN numbers, I think. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, of course, step one would be to see how it was entered -- why it was entered as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, yeah, I mean, that's not -- we can't -- I mean, without -- I mean, I suppose we could find out, but, Your Honours, in any event, that is already an exhibit and that's all we need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I just want you to look at two more documents very briefly on the question of payment, and then we will move on to a another topic. This is actually a Defence document with the ERN 198D1, and it was tab 62 of their bundle, so you've probably got it in hard copy, Mr. Bjelosevic. 65 ter, sorry. Not ERN. That's apparently a payment order for the various SJBs that came within the CSB Doboj area. Is that -- is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lower right-hand corner? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So, in fact, you did see payment documents, didn't you, because you were obliged to sign off on them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw the ones I signed. No denying that. But this ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it's been exhibited, so can I ask that -- and this is from the Defence, so I'm not sure whether this falls into the category of the same documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P02329.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally, can we just look at one other payment slip which is the ... 20112. And, sorry, it's tab 24J. Now, this is Mr. Savic. Salary payment for April and May 1992 is how the document is headed. Dinars, 100.000, which, from the sound of it, is not as much as one might think. But whose -- who is the signature? Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at it, and it says Milan Savic in the lower right-hand corner, but I'm not sure that this was his signature, unless he signs his name in two different ways. Cashier, I cannot identify that person's signature. And then on the left-hand side there is another official. I cannot recognise these signatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Even with inflation being what it was, do you know why Mr. Savic was receiving 100.000 dinars in -- for his salary in April and May?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he received this from, believe me, and why. Well, you see that this ... I don't know. I see what is written here. To who, Milan Savic. And personal income for April and May 1992, and the amount, the signature cannot be identified. Unless he signed his names in two different ways, I think ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... well, that's not -- I don't think I need to see that any further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you can put that away. Let's move on to a different topic, and that's really instructions and orders from Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we leave this topic, Ms. Korner, I'd like to try and sum up with the witness a bit about his knowledge of the existence of this special unit. Many of the documents which we saw in the last session just now were making reference either to a special unit or a special group, and also to the special police, and I'm unsure about what your testimony is in relation to these groups. So could you please summarize to the Chamber what was your knowledge in the spring of 1992 about the existence in Doboj of something called either a special group, or a special unit, or the special police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards certain documents that are related to that topic, I have spoken about each and every one of these documents. But by way of a summary, I know that in the public security station there was a special purpose unit that, as such, had not been prescribed within establishment as a special purposes unit. That was in all stations. And that unit was made up of regular policemen. The most able policemen were selected for certain activities and specialized activity. If there were to be a serious disruption in law and order or in some other possible emergencies, they would get together and go as such a unit. They also received certain training. I know that that existed within stations, and I know that in the beginning of 1992 this unit was engaged in reinforced checks in town. This was already in March. And I know that the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for the purposes of those units, they brought to the stations camouflage uniforms for these men. From time to time, they were engaged as this kind of special purposes unit, but, otherwise, they worked as regular policemen within those stations from which they had come. I don't know whether I've been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have provided some details about this. But let me just be sure that I understood it correctly, Mr. Bjelosevic. Are we to understand that in -- in all or at least in most of the seven SJBs which fell under the jurisdiction of the Doboj CSB, such special purposes police units were assigned and ready to go into action whenever needed? But outside such actions, they were just regularly -- regular policemen; but when special action, special purposes actions were needed, then these police officers would assume their role in those units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But let me correct you: There were nine stations within the CSB Doboj, not seven. For the rest, that's right. There were the regular forces dealing with ordinary duties, and there was this group, a part who would be called in as the need arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, if I understood you correctly, this was a system that was already in place from before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if we go back to the documents that we saw in the last session, reference was made to something called a Special Group. My question to you now is: Would the Special Group be an example of these special purposes units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The lists we were looking at, which specifically mention the Special Group, I said that I only recognised one of the men, Nenad Kujundzic, oh, as well as Radojica Bozovic who was name number one on the list, that those were the ones that I knew, and the other men were unknown to me. And I don't know that there was a special group or a special unit that was active within that structure at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Bjelosevic, your answer to me suggests that you knew by heart all the names of the police officers in the nine SJBs who had been assigned especially to these special purposes units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but how, then -- how, then, could you be so sure about the Special Group, which was referred to in this document, was not a special purposes unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this involves a station which was headquartered together with the centre, I would identify or recognise the individuals on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did there exist in April and May 1992 a special purposes unit in the Doboj SJB? And did you know the names of the officers who had been assigned to that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As part of the active police force, I did know some of the men from the Doboj Station, and they existed, as such, in the month of April. As for the month of May, the circumstances were completely different, and the structure was significantly increased through the reserve force. As I said, I don't recognise any of the names on the list, save for the names under numbers 1 and 11, and I'm referring to the document which reads: "Special Unit" -- "Special Group."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If we look at the other documents that were shown to us in the last session which refer to a special unit - we saw two or three payrolls to members of special units - would those units be identical to the special purposes unit to which you have now made reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to the personnel, the police officers, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me for drilling around in this matter, Mr. Bjelosevic, but, you see, your evidence is crucial for us to understand what the situation was in Doboj in the spring of 1992. You're telling us that there was something called special purposes units and that such units were composed of members of the regularly -- of the regular police forces in each of the SJBs and that these units would be called into function as the need arose. So this leaves the impression with the Court that in all of the nine SJBs there were a small number of police officers who had been assigned membership of these units and that they would enter into action upon the orders of their superior. Then we have evidence about something which is called a Special Group. And your evidence is that you knew the names of some of the members of this Special Group but that you were otherwise unaware of the existence. Then yet other documents made reference to something called special units. And here again you say that you had no knowledge of any such group -- or any such special units. This is a very confusing picture, and the assumption that would be obvious to make - perhaps wrongly - would be that the groups to which we have seen reference in these documents - special groups, special units - were, in fact, the special purposes units to which you yourself made reference in the beginning. So let me start out by asking you now again: Is that a misrepresentation of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is, and I'll tell you why. If you look at the head count on the list which reads "Special Group," and if you look at the head count on the list which read "Special Unit," neither the head count nor the personnel themselves add up. Therefore, my conclusion is that this is not in any way the prolonged or carried-over form of what was previously the special purposes unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So the Special Groups or the Special Units to which the documents referred are completely different than other groups than those whom we have been -- whom have been referred to as special purposes units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my conclusion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well then. The next question obviously is: If you then claim that you were unaware of the existence of these foreign groups, for lack of any better expression, that is to say, the special groups or the special units, they may have been formed at the SJB level or even at the CSB level as a reaction to some of the problems that were imminent at the time. But you, as chief of the CSB, were you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not set up at the level of the CSB because there was no one to do so in view of the fact that the centre was not operational. At the level of the station itself, there was one point where the station had around 2.200 [as interpreted] police officers at its disposal. Given that various regrouping was going on in different periods for different purposes as dictated by various actions, I don't know exactly how it all unfolded. There were great many people. They were ten reserve stations. Now, how they went about organising these individuals and deploying them to the battlefield, that's something that I wouldn't know, not in detail.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes the number is 1.200 policemen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let me add this: Now that I looked at these lists, one thing that strikes me as confusing is that I can't seem to be able to recognise the signatures at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, let us just conclude, then, that, in your evidence, it was possible that special groups and also special units could have been formed at the SJB level but that you were just not sure about whether this, in fact, had happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's roughly how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let us then move to the last group, the Special Police. I think Ms. Korner asked you whether the group in Doboj, which was referred to as Special Police, was, in fact, a formation similar and parallel to the Special Police in Banja Luka, and I think that your answer was negative. So if we go back to the beginning of this matter, was there, at any point, a Special Police formed in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was formed and how long it operated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think it was in early October 1992 that a Special Police detachment was set up as part of a Special Police brigade of the MUP of Republika Srpska. The detachment was stationed in Doboj and deployed as per orders and authorisations from the commander of the special brigade, Milenko --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Karasik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what was the name of the head of the detachment in Doboj, of the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At first it was Milorad Radulovic. And Nenad Gojkovic replaced him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That was all I wanted to know about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just -- just so you understand, Mr. Bjelosevic, however, we suggest that, from what one can see on the papers and the evidence, that, in fact, there was a Special Police - whatever name it had - led by Mr. Karagic operating through April through to August, whenever. Long before -- or before the October Special Police.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't deny that. What I'm saying is that I don't know. I know that Karagic did have a unit of his, which operated within the army for a while and then within the police reserve force of the Doboj Station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I do want to leave the topic. I want to look now, please, at the question of orders that came from Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at a document which was a Defence document. It's 1D0046.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's actually in -- in was in their -- it's in their bundle, Mr. Bjelosevic, at tab 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 47. This is the 15th-of-May order which is number 1 of 91 -- of 9 -- sorry, 92, it looks like, or it's 01, which means the minister, we've been told, 1/92. And I think you looked at it before. And it's about the setting up of war units. Now, I want to understand, please, from you which orders you got at the time and which you say you didn't. Did you get this order from Mr. Stanisic dated the 15th of May on or about the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, though I don't know when it reached us exactly. I said earlier on that the deputies went to attend an Assembly meeting at Pale. They flew in by helicopter, and I think that it was on their way back that some of them brought it along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So this -- when you say "on their way back," they went to see Mico Stanisic in his headquarters in Pale? Or in the office of the MUP. Is that what you're saying? Well, not Mico -- maybe not him personally, but his assistants or whoever.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputies went to attend an Assembly session, and they were taken over there by helicopter by the army. And their presence at the assembly session was seen as an opportunity, since the communication lines were down, the telefax wasn't functioning, et cetera, to give them copies to take along, and as they returned, among other things, they brought along this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. I know that's what you're saying. What I want to know is, Who did they tell you had given them these documents? How did they get them? Did they get them from Mico Stanisic himself or from one of his assistant ministers or from his secretary? Who?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't given this in person either. As I returned to my office, my secretary handed me over an envelope containing a number of documents, including this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Look, please, at the next document in this sequence which is at -- it's back to the documents we've put in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's at tab 18 of our documents, and it is P459, thank you. Oh, 559. P455.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now this is based on the same decision by Mico Stanisic, and he appoints you to the position of chief of the Doboj CSB and then member of the Serbian Republic, et cetera, of the staff, "... command and control of the overall ministry of interior forces," and it puts you in -- appoints you to the staff for command and control of the ministry's forces. Now, did you get that one? And, if so, was that at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think the documents arrived together. If you recall, I did say that the defence exercise [as interpreted] was priority number one, and that's how matters were put in place. That's how the structure was established, and that's how the tasks were set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I note that the -- on 74, 7, it's recorded "the defence exercise." I don't ... I don't think that's what the witness says. So, please, if you can verify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said you thought the documents arrived together. What did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that I thought the documents arrived together. And that, as I said earlier, defence, as such, was priority number one. And I think that it transpires from the order that this is how matters were arranged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And third document in this sequence, please, is P564; 20A of our binder. This, again, refers back to that first order, 15th of May. It's addressed to the five CSBs. Signed by Mico Stanisic, apparently. Did you get that in the same batch from your deputies when they returned from Pale?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, is it something that you've seen before? Because if we look at the top, somebody has written, "Was not given to Doboj; sent by courier."

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I want to know is, according to you, it was impossible for you to get to Pale except by this helicopter. I say "you"; anybody who was in Doboj to get to Pale. How did the courier get from Pale up to Doboj on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who's to say that the courier did arrive? He could not have, need not have arrived. Who knows through which routes and when it reached us. It is a generally-known fact that it was only on the 28th of June that passage was possible and only under armed escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't -- may I say straightaway, Mr. Bjelosevic, I don't accept that at all. Difficult it may have been, but I suggest to you that there was communication, even while the corridor operations were going on, by courier and indeed by phone and special radios. And I say -- well, I say, isn't this an example of exactly that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell that you, indeed, are not right at all when you say that it was possible to get through. I'd really like to see who took that route going from Sarajevo to Doboj at the time, unless the courier took a helicopter as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were shown originally a note of a meeting of the Doboj Crisis Staff, and this is how you came up with -- you gave the account of how you received these documents. Can you give us a rough idea of when the Assemblymen, the deputies to the Assembly, went off and collected these documents, having attended the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Who were the Assemblymen who went there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a few Assemblymen from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Mr. Joldic Miodrag.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there was Mr. Mladenko Vasiljevic. Those were the MPs from Doboj. There was a military helicopter, and I don't think that it was only these three men who were in the helicopter. There were other Assemblymen who were taken to that session who came from that area. I don't know whether they actually went. I'm just saying who the MPs from Doboj were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see the -- the evidence shows that the 16th Session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska took place on the 12th of May in Banja Luka. The next session, the 17th Session, only took place in July, 24th to 26th of July, in Jahorina. Are you saying that you didn't get any of these decisions until July?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when I got them. I've already said that I don't know when I got them, but I found them on my desk, and the secretary explained to me how they were brought there, that they were brought by the Assemblymen who were in Pale and who brought them from there. Perhaps that may be important for you now, but at that point in time it wasn't really important for me. The men were up there, and they brought this mail, and it really wasn't important for me to deal with any details and to remember it, but I'm just telling you how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's take this in stages, shall we, Mr. Bjelosevic. You said on more than one occasion this helicopter went off, there was no method of getting to Pale because of the corridor, no communication. In July, on the 24th of July, 26th of July, the corridor was open, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, you had gone up to Belgrade to attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it is absolutely inconceivable, isn't it, that you didn't get all these earlier decisions until the 24th -- after the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I said. I am just saying that I don't know the exact date when this arrived and - I repeat - how I received these documents. You are forcing me now to say a date which I simply cannot recall. And I just don't want to say anything, because that would not be serious on my part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm just asking you how it is that you said over and over again that it was when the local deputies went to attend the Assembly is when you first got these decisions of Stanisic. Because it's not possible, is it, Mr. Bjelosevic? That cannot be the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what you wish to achieve by all of this. I keep telling you how I found the documents in my office and what my secretary said to me on that occasion, that the documents were brought by the MPs when they were in Pale, where they went by helicopter. I really don't know what the point is. I don't know what you're getting at. I really don't know what else to answer. I don't see what the point is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The point is, Mr. Bjelosevic, that I suggest that throughout the whole of your evidence, virtually from when you started, you have attempted to distance yourself from any responsibility for the appalling events that took place in Doboj. That's the suggestion that I'm making to you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you are entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you did, in fact, did you not, carry out Mico Stanisic's instructions, because the police in Doboj were organised into these, what I'm calling generally, wartime units.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police operated as a detachment. It operated as a unit. What you're trying to do is to break the continuity that started in early April 1992. The orders from the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were the ones setting the course of activity. You saw the orders which said that units of the TO, volunteers, et cetera, should all be admitted onto the police force. So there is a continuity of these formations from that period on. You also have the order by Mr. Stanisic. But what I'm telling is that this sort of structure was -- existed from before. We also have them in the dispatches dating from April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, I've already dealt with your attempt to take this back to Mr. Jasarevic's order before the MUP split. But you, in fact, put into execution, didn't you, because you were the only person who had the authority to do it, Mico Stanisic's order that the ministry forces should be organised into war units. You yourself put that into effect, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying to you again: Look at when the minister -- when Minister Stanisic wrote the order. Look at the date of the order. When it exactly arrived Doboj, I cannot establish the date. As for the reserve police force, it had reached very high levels, and I know that I discussed the subject with the chief of the station as well and that that comes from these two dispatches, namely, that units of the TO, volunteers, et cetera, become part of the reserve police units. You see, you have ample evidence to that effect that it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry, the main point of the answer was not recorded. The witness said something I don't want to say because we can clarify that with the witness. "As for the reserve force, it had reached very high levels," and he said when. And it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Bjelosevic? Did you tell us when the reserve forces reached a very high level?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said that it was before that order, that this increase took place in April. And already by the end of April and in May, at the beginning of May, rather, it was a very large number of people. It was the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said another thing. When I spoke -- when I saw what was going on, I talked about this to the chief of the police station and I discussed the subject. I said it was dangerous. I said that it was something that was difficult to keep under control. And he said, We have the order. All the stations received the order of the then-ministry to act in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So that you understand clearly, I suggest, as that document we looked at that says "send by courier to Doboj," you got -- you were there and you got these documents at or about the time they were issued by Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now can we look, please, at the functioning of the CSB Doboj, which you say did not function between the 3rd of May and the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, first of all, please, at -- it's really a continuation of the earlier documents that we just looked at. 20005 at tab 22 of our documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you said something, Mr. Bjelosevic, which the interpreter didn't catch because my microphone was on.

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked whether it -- oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have to look at it on the screen. That's a document dated the 21st of May. Handwritten: "Sent to the Serbian MUP Security Services Centre, National Security Service" and appears to be signed. That your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, down here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So on the 21st of May you were asking Banja Luka, with whom you had communications, to forward the telegram to the MUP headquarters in Pale to check on a Dutch correspondent apparently named E.L.M. Robert. And someone else called Dulmers. Or was it the same person?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the middle, along that vertical line, the letters are missing and I'm trying to decipher what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the second page of the document is a better or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I've just noticed. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. It's in fact a Mr. -- I'm so sorry, it's a Mr. Robert E.L.M. Dulmers, so it is the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I was suggesting that in fairness to the witness the second page should be shown to him so he can read as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm still on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of the Serbian -- of the Serbian original. It's been copied on two pages. It's the very same document, but on the second page is a better copy of the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Sorry. Okay. Sorry, yes, could we have a look at the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This can be seen ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anyhow, it's all about doing a check on some Dutch journalist called Dulmers - and I apologize to him if he's still around the place - and you're asking Banja Luka -- well, you're asking Banja Luka SNB to give you information and also asking that it be forwarded to the MUP headquarters. Now, Mr. Bjelosevic, according to you, during the whole of May you're off doing your vital duties with the military. How come, on the 21st of May, four days later, after the last document we saw from the MUP, you're writing to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you please have a look at who this is addressed to. Once again. What do you think? Why would we be sending this to the Banja Luka centre if we had communication with Pale?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I -- I think you're -- with respect, Mr. Bjelosevic, you're trying to sidetrack the issue again. I want to know how it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, you have to understand that there is an interpretation of what you are asking. And the interpretation might not be exactly what you have said. I mean, which is only normal because it's the interpretation. Therefore, I don't think that it's appropriate that you accuse the witness of trying to sidetrack you because he might not have heard your actual question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mr. Zecevic. I accept the criticism.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelosevic, the question I asked - and I'll ask it slowly so that I hope there will be no misinterpretation - is what you are doing back in the CSB Doboj on the 21st of May, when, according to you, throughout May, you were off doing your vital military duties?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have followed my previous remarks, you could have noted or, rather, you could have heard that I stated then, and I repeat that now, from time to time I did come to my office. That is where I familiarized myself with some security information that was collected by the service, and then from there I went to the command post where we compared data, conducted analyses, and so on. I never stated that I never entered the police building and my office throughout the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wasn't it possibly more important, given the situation in Doboj, that you should be dealing with the clear and evident problems and violence that was going on in Doboj, rather than being with the military?

utterances.speaker: ANDRIJA BJELOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several reasons for why I behaved as I did at the time. One of the reasons is that, indeed, the CSB had lost its territory. There wasn't any. We had part of the Doboj municipality. The second important reason was lack of personnel. The third important reason is that defence is the number one priority. And I'm going back to Lisica's suggestions, the suggestions of General Lisica, when he said, Who are you going to keep law and order for if there's no one there? And the man was quite right. And the fourth I'm referring to is that the Crisis Staff -- and I'm not criticising them. They ordered what they ordered rightly. The municipality has its territory, the public security station has its territory, and they're the ones who are supposed to do their job ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's clear, isn't it, that the SNB is working in May? Can we have a look at who else was working, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Could I again ask that this document be marked for identification.
